summary: Describes how network virtualization overlays running Ethernet VPN (EVPN) can be connected to a wide area network to extend Layer 2 connectivity for some tenants. It analyzes interaction with other Layer 2 VPN technologies used in the WAN.

plainLanguage.summary: Separate virtual networks in data centers can be joined across long distances, as if they were one local network.

questions: how to extend layer 2 across data centers
what is evpn data center interconnect
what is an interconnect ethernet segment
what is the unknown mac route in evpn
subtitle: How EVPN-based data center overlays are joined to a WAN, with gateways that stitch the two sides together.

tldr.problem: EVPN works well as the control plane for network virtualization overlays inside a data center, but it cannot always be extended straight into a WAN that already runs VPLS, PBB-VPLS, EVPN or PBB-EVPN.
tldr.mechanism: Gateways (GWs) sit between the data center and the WAN, either as a separate system from the WAN edge router (decoupled) or merged with it (integrated). They use an Interconnect Ethernet Segment (I-ES) for multihoming and an Unknown MAC Route to keep MAC scale down.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes several interconnect options and the extensions needed for them. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Unknown MAC Route
facts.value: MAC length 48, MAC address 0, ESI set to the GW's I-ESI

today: RFC 9014 is a Proposed Standard from May 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the reference for the GW-based DCI options for EVPN-Overlay networks that it describes.

sections.title: Connecting Overlays to the WAN
sections.content:
RFC 8365 describes using Ethernet VPN (EVPN, RFC 7432) as the control plane for Network Virtualization Overlays (NVOs) in a data center, with VXLAN, NVGRE or MPLS over GRE as the data plane. That model may not extend easily into the Wide Area Network (WAN), because a service provider may already run VPLS, PBB-VPLS, EVPN or PBB-EVPN there.

A Gateway (GW) function is required in those cases. RFC 8365 describes two Data Center Interconnect (DCI) families, "DCI using GWs" and "DCI using ASBRs", and this RFC specifies the GW family. If the GW and the WAN Edge router are separate systems it is the decoupled solution, and if they are one system it is the integrated solution. The two can be mixed across data centers, because the procedures are local to the redundant GWs of each DC.

The extensions defined here are the Interconnect Ethernet Segment (I-ES), the use of the Unknown MAC Route (UMR) in DCI, and the processing of EVPN routes on GWs that connect EVPN-Overlay to EVPN-MPLS or to another EVPN-Overlay network.
sections.plainLanguage: A data center has its own fast network, but the wide-area network between cities works differently. Gateways are the translators standing between them.

sections.title: Decoupled Interconnect and Its Handoffs
sections.content:
In the decoupled model the GW and WAN Edge functions are different systems. It suits networks where the EVPN-Overlay provider and the WAN provider are different entities and a clear demarcation is needed. The requirements are a simple handoff so QoS and security are easy to enforce, independence from the WAN's L2VPN technology, multihoming with per-service load balancing, Ethernet OAM and CFM between GW and WAN Edge, and some optional GW optimizations.

There are two handoff choices. With a VLAN-based handoff, each MAC-VRF in the GW connects to a VSI or MAC-VRF in the WAN Edge router using a matching C-TAG VLAN ID or S/C-TAG combination. It gives the best demarcation and needs no control plane interaction between providers, but the provisioning overhead is high. The GW acts as a regular NVE toward the DC.

With a PW-based handoff over MPLS, the GW and WAN Edge use FEC128-based or FEC129-based pseudowires. A FEC128 PW needs a matching VCID on both sides, and with FEC129 and BGP auto-discovery the VPLS-ID MUST match. This scales better than C-TAG handoff and needs less provisioning than a combined C/S-TAG handoff, with a single PW between each MAC-VRF and peer VSI.
sections.plainLanguage: When two companies run the two sides, they need a clear border. The border can be a numbered lane on a shared road (a VLAN) or a dedicated private tunnel for each customer (a pseudowire).

sections.title: Multihoming and Gateway Optimizations
sections.content:
Multihoming here means connecting the DC to the WAN through more than one GW. The GWs are provisioned with a unique Ethernet Segment for each WAN interconnect, the I-ES, whose identifier is the I-ESI, configured administratively. Type 0 is RECOMMENDED for the I-ESI. In the decoupled model the GWs MUST follow the single-active procedures of RFC 8365, which means per-service load balancing, and MAC addresses learned on the handoff links are advertised with the I-ESI in the ESI field.

Three optional GW optimizations are described. MAC address advertisement control uses the Unknown MAC Route (UMR), a regular EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement route with MAC length 48, MAC address 0 and the ESI set to the GW's I-ESI. An NVE that understands it sends unknown unicast frames to a GW, so the GWs need not flood every WAN MAC address into the DC. Local policy decides whether MACs, the UMR, or both are advertised.

ARP/ND flooding control has the GW build a Proxy ARP/ND cache, so requests from the WAN can be answered without flooding the DC. Failure handling follows RFC 7432: the GW detecting a failure withdraws the EVPN routes, and individual AC or PW failures may be found with Ethernet CFM or with LDP PW Status bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Having two doors between the schools means that if one is blocked, the other works. The gateways also keep a cheat sheet of who lives where, and send unknown visitors to the front desk instead of shouting down every hallway.

sections.title: Integrated Interconnect: VPLS and PBB-VPLS
sections.content:
When one organization runs both DC and WAN, the GW and WAN Edge PE can be one router, which saves cost, but there is no longer an explicit demarcation link. The integrated solution needs control and data plane interworking with the WAN's L2VPN technology, multihoming, end-to-end MAC Mobility and Static MAC protection where EVPN-MPLS is used in the WAN, and independent inclusive multicast trees in the WAN and the DC.

For VPLS, each GW has a MAC-VRF per EVI with two split-horizon groups: VPLS PWs in the WAN group and overlay tunnel bindings (VXLAN, NVGRE) in the DC group. Traffic received in a group is never forwarded to a member of the same group. A GW is not allowed to have both an EVPN binding and a PW to the same far end in one MAC-VRF. If both come up, the EVPN binding wins and the PW is brought down. Only single-active multihoming is supported, since VPLS has no all-active mode, and the non-DF GW blocks the WAN PWs.

For PBB-VPLS, the B-component follows RFC 7041, and the I-component instances become EVI instances with EVPN-Overlay bindings. Many MAC-VRFs can share one B-component, which saves PWs. If a PW exists between two GWs, an EVPN binding to the same far end is kept down. Only single-active multihoming is supported, and the non-DF MUST NOT advertise EVPN MAC/IP routes for MACs learned from the WAN.
sections.plainLanguage: When one company owns both sides, the gateway can be the same machine. It makes sure a message is never sent back into the group it came from, and never travels two ways at once, which would deliver duplicates.

sections.title: EVPN-MPLS and PBB-EVPN Interconnect
sections.content:
If the WAN runs EVPN-MPLS, an end-to-end EVPN solution is possible. The GWs MUST keep separate BGP sessions to the DC and to the WAN, and routes sent to the WAN SHOULD carry a different Route Distinguisher than those sent to the DC. Received routes are never reflected: Ethernet A-D, ES and Inclusive Multicast routes are consumed locally, and MAC/IP routes are re-advertised with the GW's own RD, the ESI set to the I-ESI, the Ethernet tag, MAC and IP kept, and a new label. That label is a local 20-bit value toward the WAN or a DC-global 24-bit value toward the DC for VNI encapsulations.

Each GW keeps two flooding lists per MAC-VRF, EVPN-Overlay and EVPN-MPLS, each in its own split-horizon group. A GW includes its DC peer GW only in the EVPN-MPLS list by default, to avoid loops and duplicates. This option supports both single-active and all-active multihoming, using RFC 7432 DF election, backup-path and aliasing procedures. On the non-DF in single-active mode, ingress and egress forwarding on the overlay bindings MUST be blocked. In all-active mode, the DF MUST add the I-ESI label when sending BUM traffic received from the overlay to the peer GW, so the peer does not send it back.

MAC Mobility procedures are not modified. An intra-DC move keeps the MAC on the same I-ES and is not a mobility event, while a move between the WAN and the DC, or between DCs, is one. The sticky-bit indication MUST be propagated between domains. The UMR also helps in all-active cases: without it, an NVE that has not yet learned a MAC would flood the packet to both GWs, which would both forward it and duplicate it.

Compared to "DCI using ASBRs", the benefits include support for local attachment circuits on GWs, different data plane encapsulations in the DC and WAN, independent multicast trees, MPLS label aggregation, no propagation of intra-DC MAC moves, and proxy ARP/ND. PBB-EVPN works similarly, with EVPN running independently in the I-component and B-component MAC-VRFs and C-MACs learned from the B-component treated as local for mobility. It supports single-active and all-active multihoming.
sections.plainLanguage: When both sides speak the same language, the gateway just passes messages along, rewriting the return address so it looks like the sender. It also marks messages so that its partner gateway does not send copies back into the school where they started.

sections.title: EVPN-VXLAN Interconnect and VNI Translation
sections.content:
If the WAN also uses overlay tunnels, the procedures of the EVPN-MPLS option apply, with EVPN-VXLAN substituted. VXLAN has no ESI labels, so the GWs use the "Local Bias" procedures from RFC 8365 for split horizon between peer GWs.

VNIs are globally significant within each DC, and the GW translates them at the DC boundary and also translates the tunnel source IP, using its own address as the BGP next hop toward the interconnect network. NVEs inside a DC only ever see one VNI space. In the interconnect network there are two options. With globally unique VNIs, GWs and PEs agree on a common VNI for an EVI, and the RT can be derived from it. For example, VNI-10 in NVO-1 and VNI-20 in NVO-2 would both be mapped to VNI-100. With downstream-assigned VNIs, each GW can translate to a locally assigned VNI, which need not be agreed across all GWs and PEs, and the GWs and PEs MUST use proper RTs to import and export routes. GWs SHOULD support multiple VNI spaces per EVI.
sections.plainLanguage: Each school numbers its classrooms differently. The gateway keeps a translation table, so room 10 in one school and room 20 in the other can both be called room 100 when talking between schools.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC applies existing specifications, so the security considerations of RFC 7432, RFC 8365, RFC 7623, RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 apply wherever those technologies are used. It argues that GWs give better per-tenant security than ASBRs, because GWs do a MAC lookup on frames from the WAN and can filter unwanted frames, filter frames whose source MAC matches a protected MAC in the DC, and apply MAC-duplication procedures. ASBRs forward by label or VNI swap and usually cannot see the encapsulated frames.

The GW optimizations also protect the DC. The UMR keeps NVEs from being overwhelmed by MAC/IP routes learned from the WAN, and ARP/ND flooding control can suppress broadcast storms from the WAN. The decoupled solution is typically easier to protect, since each GW has one logical link to one WAN PE, whereas an integrated GW has logical links to all WAN PEs attached to the tenant. In either model, proper control plane and data plane policies should protect the DC.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway can check every visitor at the door, so it can turn away bad ones. Keeping the cheat sheet short and answering questions itself also stops crowds from the outside from flooding the school.

items.title: Decoupled
items.text: GW and WAN Edge are separate systems, linked by a VLAN or PW handoff with a clear demarcation.

items.title: Integrated
items.text: GW and WAN PE are one router, with no explicit demarcation link between DC and WAN.
